# Catching what network policy lets through

<p class="dev-note-deck">An experiment in what a complete security layer for OpenShell agents can look like.</p>

</div>

OpenShell decides where an agent may connect. That stops a lot: an agent can't reach a host its policy doesn't name. But much of the harm an agent can do happens over connections the policy allows.

An agent that may call a model API can paste a cloud key into its prompt. A web page or a tool result can tell the agent to do something you never asked for. An MCP server can quietly change what one of its tools says it does, after you approved it. In each case the agent talks to an approved host, so network policy can't tell the difference.

We wanted to see what a complete answer would take: not one filter, but everything a security team needs when an agent misbehaves. So we built a working prototype, OpenAgentSec, around stock OpenShell and tested it. It plugs in only through OpenShell's [supervisor middleware](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/extensibility/supervisor-middleware) and the events OpenShell already emits.

!!! abstract "TL;DR"

    - **Hypothesis:** a complete security layer (inspection, local decisions, evidence and verified response) can be built around stock OpenShell, using only its extension points, without slowing agents down by more than 100 ms.
    - **Result:** mostly supported. OpenShell needed no changes, the added latency was 40 to 66 ms, every tool-poisoning case was caught, and responses were verified by an independent check.
    - **Gap:** pattern rules caught only 12 of 18 prompt-injection cases. The misses show where models and the harness need to help.

## What we built

We started from the questions a security team asks when an agent misbehaves, and built one piece of the prototype for each:

| Question | What the prototype does |
|---|---|
| What is this agent sending and receiving? | Inspects each request and reply inside allowed connections |
| Can we stop it in time? | Decides on the host, in tens of milliseconds, without asking a central server |
| What exactly happened? | Keeps evidence: the rule that fired, the process tree, files touched and DNS lookups |
| Can we contain just this agent? | Quarantines one sandbox and leaves the others running |
| Did the response really work? | Marks it done only after an independent check reads it back |

The prototype has three parts:

| Part | Where it runs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| IPS (inspection) | On each host, as OpenShell middleware, a TLS inspector and an optional Suricata packet sensor | Reads each request and reply, checks every packet, and blocks threats |
| Agent | On each host, beside the sandboxes | Finds sandboxes, keeps their quarantine state, and carries out actions |
| Server and console | Once, centrally | Turns evidence into incidents, and lets people approve and follow responses |

It works with three projects that keep their own releases: [Agent Policy Fabric](https://github.com/NVIDIA/agent-policy-fabric) (APF) for signed per-request policy, the [OpenShell exporter](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell-Research/tree/main/projects/tools/openshell-exporter) in this repository for delivering evidence, and [Falco](https://falco.org/) as the runtime sensor.

### Built on open source

The prototype is assembled from open-source projects. We wrote the glue and the inspection; the rest is reused:

| Layer | Open-source tools | Role in the prototype |
|---|---|---|
| Sandbox | [OpenShell](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell) | Runs the agent and enforces network policy, unchanged |
| Policy | [Agent Policy Fabric](https://github.com/NVIDIA/agent-policy-fabric) | Signed allow, deny or ask decisions for each request |
| Network | [Suricata](https://suricata.io/), [ET Open](https://rules.emergingthreats.net/) rules, nftables | Checks every packet inline, with no way around it |
| Runtime | [Falco](https://falco.org/) | Watches the programs a sandbox runs and the files it opens |
| Telemetry | [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/), OpenInference, NVIDIA NeMo Relay | Names the models, tools and MCP servers an agent uses |
| Evidence | [OpenShell exporter](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell-Research/tree/main/projects/tools/openshell-exporter), CloudEvents, OCSF | Delivers evidence to the server and sends incidents to a SIEM |
| Detection | [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io/), OWASP Agentic Top 10, MITRE ATLAS | The rule format, and the attack catalogs the rules map to |
| Server and console | SQLite, React, React Flow | Stores incidents and draws the console and agent map |
| Sign-in | Keycloak or Dex (OIDC) | Controls who can see and approve what |
| Search and traces (optional) | OpenSearch, Langfuse | Search incidents and view agent traces |
| Supply chain | Sigstore cosign, CycloneDX | Signed images with a software bill of materials |
| Agents we tested | OpenAI Agents SDK, Hermes | Unmodified agents running under protection |

## Hypothesis

We expected that a full security layer for agents could be added to OpenShell from the outside. We broke that into four claims we could test:

| | Claim |
|---|---|
| **H1** | Inspecting what the agent sends and receives inside allowed connections stops attacks that network policy lets through: leaked secrets, prompt injection and poisoned tools. |
| **H2** | The inspection can run on OpenShell's existing extension points, with OpenShell unchanged, and add at most 100 ms at p95. |
| **H3** | Every allow or block can be decided on the host. The central server isn't needed for each request, and protection stays on if the server can't be reached. |
| **H4** | A response, such as quarantining one sandbox, can be proven: it counts as done only after an independent check reads it back, and other sandboxes keep running. |

## Theory

Why we expected this to work:

- **OpenShell already sees everything.** The supervisor handles every request the agent sends and every reply it gets. Through supervisor middleware, it asks an outside service about each one and enforces the answer. A check placed there sees the content, not just the host. (H1, H2)
- **Policy and threats are different questions.** Policy asks "is this request allowed?"; inspection asks "is this request dangerous?". If the threat check runs last and can veto, a policy allow can never let a threat through. (H1)
- **Local decisions are fast and survive outages.** A check on the same host adds milliseconds, not a network round trip, and doesn't stop working when the central server goes down. (H2, H3)
- **"Applied" isn't proof.** The component that carries out an action can be wrong about the result. A separate verifier, with permission only to read, can confirm the effect. (H4)

We also expected a limit. Rules match words and patterns, so they should miss attacks that carry intent without the usual words, or that hide data by encoding it.

## How it works

### How one request is checked

Every request the agent sends passes four checks, in this order:

1. **OpenShell policy.** Is this program allowed to reach this host?
2. **APF.** A signed policy answers allow, deny or "ask a person" for this exact request.
3. **IPS.** The inspection reads the final request: headers, body and MCP tool calls. If it finds a threat, it blocks the request, even when APF allowed it.
4. **The reply.** Model responses and tool results come back through the IPS, which checks them for prompt injection, leaked secrets and changed tool lists before the agent sees them.

Underneath, an optional [Suricata](https://suricata.io/) sensor checks every packet the sandbox sends, inline and with no bypass, using the open ET Open rules. Traffic the checks above can't read, such as raw or QUIC traffic, is denied.

The order matters. A policy can allow a request, but it can never override a threat block.

!!! example "A tool that changed after you approved it"

    You approve an MCP server with three tools. Later, the server rewrites one tool's description to tell the agent to read a credentials file. The IPS compares every tool list the server sends with the definitions you approved. It removes the changed tool before the agent sees it and opens an incident. Calls to tools that were never approved are refused before the MCP server receives them.

### Decisions stay on the host

The central server is never on the request path. If a host loses contact with it, protection keeps working for a bounded time and then denies requests, so cutting the network can't turn protection off. A quarantine is stored on the host and survives restarts.

### From a block to a response

Each block becomes a record, and the server groups records into an incident. The incident shows the agent and sandbox, the rule that fired, and what was happening around it: the process tree, files the agent touched and the DNS names it looked up.

When someone responds:

1. They see a preview of the exact action, give a reason and confirm it.
2. The console follows the action through each step: queued, delivered, accepted, applied, verified.
3. "Verified" appears only after an independent verifier reads the sandbox's state back.
4. Releasing a sandbox from quarantine needs a second person to approve.

By default, a person approves every quarantine. Administrators can make chosen critical rules quarantine automatically.

A prompt-injection block opens an incident but never quarantines the agent. Otherwise any web page could get an agent shut down by including a suspicious sentence.

## Experiment

We ran the attack, real-agent, speed and robustness tests on stock OpenShell 0.1.6, on one arm64 machine, with Docker and with Kubernetes (k3s). The offline and response tests ran on one Docker host with placeholder sandboxes:

- **Attacks:** a corpus of hostile and harmless agent traffic, mapped to the [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/), run through a protected sandbox. It runs on every change, and its pass rates may never drop.
- **A real agent:** an unmodified OpenAI Agents SDK agent doing a task through the IPS, with an unapproved MCP tool, a changed tool definition and a credential planted in a model reply.
- **Speed:** the same fixed mix of requests with and without protection, three runs per platform, comparing the 95th percentile.
- **Robustness:** attempts to bypass the checks, load, sandbox lifecycle and restarting the supervisor.
- **Response:** quarantining one sandbox while a second keeps running, then checking the result with the independent verifier.

## Results

### What we measured

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Added latency at p95, Docker, under a fixed mixed load | 40 to 46 ms (our limit is 100 ms) |
| Added latency at p95, Kubernetes (k3s) | 51 to 66 ms |
| Tool-poisoning cases (OWASP Agentic ASI04) | 5 of 5 detected |
| Goal-hijack and prompt-injection cases (ASI01) | 12 of 18 blocked |
| A real agent (OpenAI Agents SDK) on stock OpenShell | It finishes its task. Its call to an unapproved MCP tool is refused, and a credential planted in a model reply never reaches it |
| Bypass, load, lifecycle and supervisor restart on Docker | 84 of 84 checks passed; every k3s phase passed |
| Harmless requests that failed under load, after the fix below | 0 |
| Detection rules | 85 signed rules covering all ten OWASP Agentic categories and 52 MITRE ATLAS techniques |

### Hypotheses

| | Result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **H1** | Every tool-poisoning case and the planted credential were stopped, but 6 of 18 prompt-injection cases got through. | Partly supported |
| **H2** | OpenShell unchanged, and the added latency stayed under 100 ms on both platforms. | Supported |
| **H3** | No request waited on the server. With the server unreachable, protection kept working for a bounded time and then denied requests. The quarantine survived restarts. | Supported |
| **H4** | The quarantine ended the sandbox's run, the second sandbox was unaffected, and only the verifier's readback marked it verified. | Supported on Docker |

### A surprise from the packet sensor

Latency was under the limit from the start, but a few harmless requests kept failing in every protected run: up to 7 in a 30-second workload on Docker and up to 3 on Kubernetes. The cause was an interaction between two layers. When our TLS inspector closed a connection first, Suricata sometimes kept that connection in a closing state and dropped new connections from the same address and port for about a minute. When the supervisor reused that port, the request timed out.

We changed the inspector to let the other side close first. After the fix, no harmless request failed in any protected run on Docker or Kubernetes. Layering security tools adds protection, but the layers also interact in ways you only find under load.

### What still gets through

The prediction about rules held. The prototype missed:

- data leaked through a planted Markdown image link;
- instructions injected into the user's own turn;
- secrets the agent encodes before sending, as an earlier Dev Note showed in [The leak is coming from inside the sandbox](2026-09-26-network-redaction-is-not-enough.md);
- injections with no override words, such as a persona jailbreak or a request to repeat the system prompt.

There are also limits on what it can inspect. It reads HTTPS requests up to 64 KiB, and it withholds WebSockets, compressed bodies and QUIC rather than letting them through unchecked. MCP over stdio isn't covered. The server is a single writer with no high availability. OpenAgentSec is a research prototype and isn't qualified for production use.

## Conclusion

A complete security layer for agents can be built around OpenShell today, without changing it: inspection inside allowed traffic, decisions on the host, evidence people can follow, and responses that are proven. What we learned:

- **OpenShell's extension points are enough.** Middleware sees every request and reply, and the supervisor enforces the answer. We didn't have to change OpenShell to add deep inspection.
- **Where a decision is made matters.** Deciding on the host keeps latency low and keeps protection on when the network fails.
- **A block is the start, not the end.** Most of the work went into evidence and responses that people can trust.
- **Pattern rules hit a ceiling.** The misses above need a model that reads intent, and help from the harness, which sees what the network never does.
